Brainwallet.io uses 262,144 iterations of the time and memory-intensive scrypt key derivation function to generate brainwallets. The salts are used to thwart brute force attacks. Brainwallet generation takes place in your browser, and no information ever gets sent to our server.

https://brainwallet.io

The idea of using scrypt for brainwallets was first implemented by warpwallet, and they get all of the credit for this. I am offering an alternate solution that requires additional salt options for enhanced security.

I encourage developers to review my code to verify the security of this website. All source code is available on GitHub.
What's your reasoning behind asking for name, phone #, etc? Can you link to the GitHub repo?

The reason your personal information is used as salts is simply because these are things that you won't forget. Even if you don't take the necessary precautions to create and memorize a strong passphrase, using your personal information as a salt creates an added layer of security that requires an attacker to personally target you, instead of cracking your brainwallet in a wide, generic sweep of all passphrases.

You also have the option to chose other types of salts. Instead of your personal info, you can input a username, password, and PIN code of your choice. Again, the idea here is to use something that you won't forget, such as your ATM PIN code.

If you are not comfortable with either of these salt options, then you can input your own generic salt.

The GitHub repository is located here: https://github.com/routman/brainwallet.io
Figured that was why, but wanted to hear you explain it. Now I just need to try and remember my phone number. ;)

If the passphrase has enough entropy you don't have to worry about brute force attacks.

I use diceware to make all my passphrases. A simple 7 word passphrase selected from the 7,660 word diceware list, all lower case with spaces between the words, has 128 bits of entropy and is trivial to memorize. It might be useful to your users to host a copy of the diceware pdf and the basic instructions (roll some six-sided dice to get a 5 digit number and search the pdf to get the listed word) to construct a really truly random passphrase.

UPDATE

A random 12-word passphrase generator has been added to brainwallet.io. It selects words from a list of 1,626 memorable words in a cryptographically random manner. This is a similar process to what Electrum uses for wallet seeds.

Humans are known to be poor entropy sources when it comes to generating random words. This should be a useful functionality for people who have doubts in the security of their passphrase.

Remember to always write down your passphrase!

The younger gamers see all of this and think it is a normal part of the industry. They just go along with it because it is all they know.
